column1: # Per-bucket native/oracle timing limits and comparison coverage (cgz-7v2.4.7,
# re-measured across all five buckets in cgz-7v2.4.9).
# Columns are tab separated:
#   bucket  max_cpu_median_ratio  max_cpu_p95_ratio  min_compared_members
# A ratio is a native thread-CPU-time percentile divided by the corresponding
# oracle thread-CPU-time percentile over the same member population, in the
# same process and build. Above 1.0 means native consumes more CPU. Wall-clock
# percentiles and every per-member wall/CPU sample remain in benchmark output
# as latency and scheduling diagnostics, but do not decide the regression gate.
# `min_compared_members` is how many of the bucket's 20 members native could lay
# out when this row was written; a member native refuses is skipped on BOTH
# sides, so the populations stay like-for-like and coverage is tracked
# separately rather than silently folded into the timing.
# ## Why per bucket
# SUCCESS_CRITERIA requires median AND p95 per size bucket so a regression
# confined to `huge` members is visible rather than averaged away. One
# whole-corpus number would let a 5x regression on 50 huge members hide behind
# 1900 small ones.
# ## Where these numbers came from
# Originally measured as wall time on aarch64-macos, pinned toolchain
# 0.17.0-dev.1516+8a4b5424d, ReleaseFast, at dd4bb2f. Sixteen runs: five
# consecutive uncontended ones, and eleven taken while other work shared the
# machine. Ranges below span ALL SIXTEEN. The later CPU-clock validation is
# recorded below; it required no threshold increase.
#   bucket   median ratio     p95 ratio        compared
# `small` median is the widest spread in the table by far - a 1.55x span
# between its quietest and busiest run, against roughly 1.2x for every other
# median. Its absolute times are in the hundreds of microseconds, small enough
# for scheduler noise to matter and large enough to be worth many samples.
# ## Headroom, and why it is this wide
# Thresholds sit roughly 40% above the highest sample in each range, matching
# the margin the first baseline gave `tiny` - its noisiest bucket - rather than
# the ~23% it gave `small`.
# That margin is not arbitrary caution. A first attempt at these rows used ~25%
# headroom and set `small` median to 2.40 against an observed 1.683 - 1.798.
# The very next run measured 2.409 and the gate went red, having caught
# nothing but a loaded laptop: every p95 in that run was elevated too, and
# native's absolute small-bucket time was ~50% above any previous run. A later
# run measured 2.614, so the reverted threshold would have failed twice. The
# first baseline had called `small` "stable to about 2%", which held across
# four quiet runs and does not hold under load.
# One machine's contention is not a bound on a CI runner's. Since the spread
# cannot be characterised by sampling harder locally, the margin has to absorb
# it. A gate that fires on noise is one that gets relaxed on first contact,
# which is the cgz-r21 failure mode this file exists to avoid.
# ## What changed since the first baseline, and why every edit here is a
# ## tightening
# The first baseline could not measure medium, large or huge AT ALL: native
# laid out none of their 20 members, so those three rows were written `0 0 0`
# as a placeholder meaning "no data". PRs #27-#30 gave native full coverage of
# every bucket, which turned those placeholders into live thresholds of zero
# and put the gate into permanent failure. That is cgz-7v2.4.9. The rows now
# carry measurements.
# The two buckets that already had numbers both IMPROVED:
# `tiny` median (1.50) and `small` median (3.80) are left alone. `small` median
# is the one that looks most obviously loose - 3.80 guarding a 1.683 - 1.798
# median - and it is exactly the row whose tightening was tried and reverted
# above. Its measured range under load reaches 2.614. Lowering it further is
# free under the editing rules and would still be wrong: there is no evidence
# it would catch a regression, and clear evidence it would fire on load.
# ## The one raise in this file, and its decision
#   small p95      4.30 -> 5.60   decided in cgz-7v2.4.14
# 4.30 came from the first baseline: four runs, one host, quiet machine,
# observed 3.457 - 3.483, set ~23% above. More evidence has since contradicted
# that sample. CI has been running `performance-baseline` on both platforms all
# along, and those logs were never read. Eight samples across four runs at or
# after dd4bb2f, every bucket at 20 of 20:
#   platform       small median    small p95
#   ubuntu-24.04   1.697           4.525   <- exceeded the old 4.30
# The threshold sat INSIDE the range of the thing it measures. One Linux sample
# violated it outright; the tightest macOS sample cleared it by 8%. 5.60 is
# ~24% over the highest of the eight, which is the headroom every other row
# carries.
# This raise is not admitting a regression, which is what the editing rule below
# exists to catch. Native did not get slower - the same code measures 2.917 on
# one runner and 4.525 on another. The number being corrected was derived from a
# sample now known to be unrepresentative. That distinction is the whole content
# of the decision, which is why it was taken as one rather than assumed.
# ## Two findings the numbers carry, which these thresholds do not endorse
# THE TINY TAIL MOVED. cgz-twy was filed on a tiny p95 of 10.2 - 13.9 in every
# one of three runs, against a median at parity. It now measures 2.5 - 3.5 in
# twelve. Something in PRs #27-#30 appears to have fixed it, but the bead stays
# open: tiny is the noisiest bucket, the comparison set also changed from 19
# members to 20, and nobody has identified the cause. `tiny` p95 is therefore
# set at 6.00 - roughly 70% above the highest sample, against the ~40% the
# other rows get - so it is not a noise trigger, while still being 3.3x
# tighter than the 20.00 it replaces. If the old tail returns, this gate goes
# red, which is what cgz-twy wants.
# THE MEDIAN NOW DEGRADES WITH SIZE: 4x on medium, 5.1x on large, 5.5x on huge,
# while the p95 ratio stays flat near 3.5 - 4.4 across every bucket. A constant
# overhead would hold the ratio steady across buckets; one that grows with
# input size while the tail does not points at a term that scales worse in
# native than in the oracle. That is cgz-7v2.4.12. Setting a huge threshold at
# 8.00 does not accept 5.5x as correct any more than the old tiny row accepted
# 13x - this gate's job is to stop things getting worse, and a threshold set
# below today's value would be red from the day it landed without making
# anything faster.
# ## Why the gate uses thread CPU time (cgz-7v2.4.15)
# The original p95 ratio divided two wall-clock tails. One loaded run produced
# a `huge` p95 of 8.942 while `medium` fell to 1.723, below its own median ratio
# of 4.229. Pairing adjacent wall samples is worse: in a controlled experiment
# with the benchmark pinned beside three competitors, paired p95 ratios reached
# 75-120 on small and 88-106 on huge because adjacent calls received different
# scheduler slices. Per-member wall medians still reached 39-102.
# Thread CPU time removes that scheduler term without hiding implementation
# work. Across three quiet and three identically loaded x86_64 runs, CPU p95
# ranges were stable: tiny 3.141-3.748 vs 3.213-3.739, small 4.351-4.601 vs
# 33504213332 then showed wall and CPU ratios agreeing within measurement noise
# on macOS aarch64 and Linux x86_64. Thus the existing limits remain valid and
# the p95 still catches CPU work confined to a bucket tail, including the shape
# that opened cgz-twy, without validation-audit's own host load deciding the
# result. Wall rows remain visible and cgz-7v2.4.16 owns abnormal wall/CPU gaps.
# ## Reproducing these numbers
# Two capture hazards, both hit while collecting the data above:
# `zig build performance-baseline -Denable-oracle=true` prints the run step's
# inherited stdout only ONCE per shell, so a loop of repeated invocations gives
# you the first run's output and four silent no-ops. Drive the built binary
# directly for repeat runs; it is the same binary the gate runs, without
# --enforce.
# The benchmark writes stdout with POSITIONAL writes. Redirected straight to a
# regular file on macOS it starts at offset 0 every run, so run 2 overwrites
# run 1 in place and the file ends up holding one run while looking like it
# holds five. Pipe through `cat` - a pipe is not seekable, so writes append.
# That is cgz-7v2.4.13.
# ## Editing rules
# LOWERING max_*_ratio, or RAISING min_compared_members, makes the gate
# stricter and needs no justification.
# RAISING a ratio is admitting a regression. LOWERING min_compared_members is
# admitting native stopped handling members it used to handle. Both require a
# decision Bead, because they are the edits that turn a red gate green without
# fixing anything.
# A bucket with no row is NOT permission: --enforce fails on a missing row for
# any bucket where native laid out at least one member. A row of zeroes is not
# permission either, and this file has learned that the hard way: zeroes read
# as a threshold of zero the moment the bucket becomes measurable.
# bucket
